profile.explanation: The paper identifies its focus as procedural fairness in service queues through social philosophy and decision theory. It proposes conceptual analysis, reconstruction of philosophical arguments, and counterexamples, and explicitly says it does not conduct an empirical experiment. This profile describes the proposed approach, not its correctness.

references.evidence_text: This conceptual paper examines procedural fairness in service queues using social philosophy and decision theory. It proposes an argument, not an empirical experiment or an already proven theorem.
references.evidence_before:
# Synthetic theoretical proposal: fair waiting as a procedural claim
This document is synthetic and prepared only for local AI conversation review.
## Aim and field
references.evidence_after:
## Central question
Under what assumptions does first-arrival service order count as procedurally fair, and when do justified exceptions undermine that claim?
## Definitions

references.evidence_before:
Arrival means entry to a publicly observable queue rather than entry to the building. Procedural fairness here means that a publicly stated rule applies equally to cases considered relevantly alike. Equal moral worth is distinguished from identical practical needs.
## Working argument
First-arrival order can protect predictability and discourage favoritism when arrival is observable, participants can access the queue and exceptional priority rules are publicly justified. These are conditional assumptions, not facts demonstrated about every institution.
references.evidence_after:
The proposal uses conceptual analysis, reconstructs arguments from selected philosophical sources and tests its definitions with counterexamples. It does not recruit participants, collect interviews, conduct statistical tests or claim to estimate the public's attitudes.
## Counterexamples
A person with an urgent accessibility need may deserve priority even when they arrived later. A person whose arrival is unobservable challenges whether the rule can be applied consistently. These examples test the scope of the proposed definition without proving a practical policy is optimal.

turns.answer: A reader could separate three claims that are often conflated: an order is predictable, similar cases get equal treatment, and a priority exception has a reason. Our conceptual contribution would be showing which premises support each claim and where one can hold without the others. A worked accessibility counterexample could make the distinction useful for reasoning; it would not demonstrate better service performance or justify any institution-specific rule.

feedback.summary: The proposal is appropriately presented as conceptual work, not as an empirical study or established result (theoretical.md, lines 4, 12, 20). The host ended the defense; topics on the central question, conditional case, counterexamples, and remaining argument work were still pending, while discussion of relevant similarity also left an acknowledged issue unresolved. Coverage indicates discussion, not validation of the argument.

strengths.text: In Q1, the probe reply gave a useful proposed test: if a case meets the stated conditions yet results in unequal treatment of relevantly similar cases, the claimed sufficient condition needs revision. It also correctly treated this as a planned argument check, not proof (theoretical.md, lines 12, 14).

In Q2, you explained how you would state normative premises, reconstruct opposing arguments charitably, and separate their premises from your objections. You also accurately acknowledged that the source comparison is not yet complete (theoretical.md, line 16).

In Q3, you explained the conceptual value of distinguishing predictability, equal treatment, and justified priority, while explicitly avoiding claims of improved service performance (theoretical.md, lines 18–20).

improvements.text: In Q1, the original answer that you would read sources and judge whether the argument is reasonable was too general to show how the planned analysis will work. The probe reply improved this, but the paper still does not identify the selected sources or explain how they will be chosen or reconstructed (theoretical.md, line 12).

In Q2, you said the source comparison remains unfinished. Prepare to describe how you will complete it; the proposal also leaves unspecified how a later policy discussion would consider exclusion and accessibility (theoretical.md, line 16).

In Q4, you offered a provisional similarity criterion and appropriately called it unresolved. Be ready to defend which differences count as morally relevant and how you will test the criterion for unfair exclusions, without presenting it as already sufficient (theoretical.md, lines 8, 20).

feedback.next_step: Before the defense, prepare a concise argument map that states your provisional relevant-similarity criterion, connects it to the proposal’s assumptions, and shows how the accessibility and unobservable-arrival cases might challenge those assumptions. Also identify the philosophical sources and basis for selecting them, and outline which alternative priority rules you plan to compare; these will help address the pending topics left when the host ended the defense.
